Orchot Tzadikim 17:2: Generosity is the trait by which a person attains great virtues. And when generosity follows a good path, it is very praiseworthy, and through it one attains many virtues in this world and in the World to Come, as it is said (Proverbs 18:16), "a man's gift makes room for him, and brings him before great men." For because of his gifts, kings and officers and every person will love him. And there is nothing in the world that brings a person to the world's love as generosity does, and in the World to Come too he will attain good reward for his gift.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:3: There are three kinds of generosity: the first, generous with money; the second, generous with the body; the third, generous with wisdom. And all three of these were found in Abraham our father: he was generous with money, as it is written (Genesis 21:33), "and he planted an eshel [tamarisk / hospitality-grove]." He was generous with his body, in that he saved Lot, his brother's son, and fought on his behalf. He was generous with his wisdom, for he taught the whole people the straight path until they converted, as it is written (ibid. 12:5), "and the souls that they had made in Charan."
Orchot Tzadikim 17:4: This trait is very praiseworthy, because through it a person is honored, as it is written (Proverbs 19:6), "many will entreat the favor of a generous man," and his words are heeded when he rebukes people to return to the service of the Blessed Creator. If he needs help, everyone will help him, and everyone will be at peace with him.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:5: And know that a gift given where it is fitting, such as charity to poor people who fear Heaven, is a hidden treasure that is never lost over the length of days, but endures forever. And this is the intent of King Solomon, peace upon him, who said (Ecclesiastes 11:1), "cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you shall find it." And the plain meaning of the verse speaks of generosity, for whoever sows kindness reaps its produce. And whoever has this trait grows rich, as it is said (Proverbs 11:24), "there is one who scatters, and yet increases"; and further it is written (ibid. 28:27), "he who gives to the poor shall not lack." And David said of generous men (Psalms 112:9), "he has scattered abroad, he has given to the needy; his righteousness endures forever."
Orchot Tzadikim 17:6: And this important trait is [counted as] a loan given to the Blessed Creator, as it is said (Proverbs 19:17), "he who is gracious to the poor lends to the Lord." And the wise man said: do kindness with whoever deserves it and with whoever does not deserve it. Its meaning: "with whoever deserves it" — let the kindness be given in its proper place; "and with whoever does not deserve it" — let it be you who is deserving of doing it. And the Sages said: whoever gives a great gift to one who requested the gift is only half generous. But the truly complete generous man is one who gives constantly, whether much or little, before he is asked.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:7: And the wise man further said: the trait of generosity depends on habit, for one is not called "generous" unless he is accustomed at every time and every hour to give generously according to his ability. For a person who gives a thousand gold pieces at once to one who deserves it is not as generous as one who gives a thousand gold pieces on a thousand separate occasions, each gold piece to whoever deserves it. For the one who gives a thousand gold pieces at once had his mind stirred to give generously, and afterward it ceased in him. And likewise regarding reward: there is no reward for one who redeems a single captive held in prison for a debt of a hundred dinars, which is enough to cover his need, equal to the reward of one who redeems ten captives, or fills the need of ten poor people with a hundred dinars, ten dinars to each. And of this our Sages said (Avot 3:15): everything depends on the abundance of the deed — and they did not say, "on the greatness of the deed."
Orchot Tzadikim 17:8: Whoever hides his eyes from charity is as though he worshipped idols, and is called "worthless," "wicked," "cruel," and "sinner." "Worthless," as it is said (Deuteronomy 15:9), "beware lest there be a worthless thought in your heart, saying, the seventh year, the year of release, is at hand, and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing." "Cruel," as it is written (Proverbs 12:10), "but the mercies of the wicked are cruel." And he denies his own lineage, that he is not of the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who were merciful (Yevamot 79a), but rather of the seed of the nations, who are cruel, as it is said (Jeremiah 50:42), "they are cruel, and will not show mercy." And whoever shows mercy is shown mercy from Heaven, as it is said (Deuteronomy 13:18), "and He will show you mercy, and have compassion upon you, and multiply you" (Shabbat 151b).
Orchot Tzadikim 17:9: And whoever gives charity to the poor with a sour face has lost his merit, even though he gives much; and he transgresses "and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him" (Deuteronomy 15:10). Better than him is one who gives a single coin to the poor man with a pleasant countenance. And it is good to give before being asked. And it is good to give in secret, as it is written (Proverbs 21:14), "a gift in secret pacifies anger." And there were those who would tie money into a garment and toss it behind them, and the poor would come and take it, so that the giver did not know to whom he gave, and the recipient did not know from whom he received, and was not ashamed (Ketubot 67b). In sum: whatever one can keep hidden, so that the poor man not know who the giver is, and the giver not know who the recipient is, he should keep hidden.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:10: And when a person gives charity, let him also do kindness together with the charity — for instance, buying with that money something the poor man needs, so the poor man not need to trouble himself; and let the rich man buy it more cheaply than the poor man could. And let the rich man be careful to give it at the time the poor man needs it, and thereby do him a kindness. And of this the prophet said (Hosea 10:12), "sow for yourselves according to righteousness, reap according to kindness." Its meaning: the reward follows the kindness.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:11: And now hear the importance of generosity and those devoted to charity, as it is written (Proverbs 14:34), "righteousness [charity] exalts a nation." Come and see how great is the power of charity, that it is placed in the right hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Psalms 48:11), "Your right hand is full of righteousness."
Orchot Tzadikim 17:12: Great is charity, for by it the Holy One, blessed be He, is praised at the time He is destined to bring salvation to Israel, as it is said (Isaiah 63:1), "I who speak in righteousness, mighty to save." Great is charity, for it grants honor and life to whoever performs it, as it is said (Proverbs 21:21), "he who pursues righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor." And why should one who pursues righteousness find [more] righteousness?! Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, provides him with money in order to make from it charity for worthy people, so as to receive reward from it. Great is charity, for by it the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to redeem Israel, as it is said (Isaiah 1:27), "Zion shall be redeemed with justice, and her returnees with righteousness." Great is charity, for by it Abraham our father was praised, as it is said (Genesis 15:6), "and he believed in the Lord, and He counted it to him as righteousness"; and it says (ibid. 18:19), "for I have known him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice, in order that the Lord bring upon Abraham that which He has spoken of him." Great is charity, for by it David king of Israel was praised, as it is said (2 Samuel 8:15), "and David executed justice and righteousness to all his people." Great is charity, for by it King Solomon, peace upon him, was praised, as it is said (1 Kings 10:9), "blessed be the Lord your God, who delighted in you, to set you on the throne of Israel; because the Lord loved Israel forever, He made you king, to execute justice and righteousness." Great is charity, for it reaches up to the Throne of Glory, as it is said (Psalms 89:15), "righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne." Great is charity, for by it Israel were praised, as it is said (Deuteronomy 6:25), "and it shall be righteousness for us, if we observe to do..." Great is charity, for by it the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to be praised on the Day of Judgment, as it is said (Isaiah 5:16), "but the Lord of Hosts is exalted through justice, and the holy God is sanctified through righteousness." Great is charity, for it accompanies the one who performs it at the time of his passing, as it is said (ibid. 58:8), "and your righteousness shall go before you; the glory of the Lord shall gather you in." Great is kindness, for by it the world was built, as it is said (Psalms 89:3), "the world is built by kindness." Therefore let a person cleave to the trait of generosity, which brings about all these good things.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:13: And he should further be generous with his money to acquire the commandments, such as Rabban Gamliel, who bought an etrog for a thousand zuz (Sukkah 41b). And he should be generous with his money to beautify the commandments, and the beautification of a commandment is worth up to a third [more of one's money] (Bava Kamma 9b).
Orchot Tzadikim 17:14: And he should be generous with his money to write and buy books, and lend them to whoever has none, as it is said (Psalms 112:3), "wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever" (Ketubot 50a). And he should be forbearing in this, not worrying if the books become worn from being studied. And he should be generous with the vessels of his house, lending them to his neighbors and acquaintances.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:15: And he should be generous in lending his money to the poor, and if his means suffice, he should lend to the rich as well. And he should be generous in his business dealings with everyone, and not be exacting with his fellow over a small matter. If he measures out wine or oil or anything else, he should not measure stingily.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:16: And he should be generous with his own body, exerting himself for every person, bearing their burdens and their load, grieving in their trouble, praying on their behalf, rejoicing in their joy, visiting the sick, and doing kindness for the dead.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:17: And above all he must be generous with his knowledge of Torah (Sukkah 49b), teaching every person understanding and drawing their hearts toward Heaven. And this is the greatest generosity of all kinds of generosity — one who gives generously of himself to a person in order to bring him to the life of the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 17:18: Even though the trait of generosity is good, one must be careful not to be a squanderer, satisfying his heart's cravings with kinds of food and drink, giving his wealth to harlots, making costly garments, and squandering it on schemes that do not lead to the fear of Heaven. A generous-hearted man must take care not to squander in vain, and not to pursue desires that bring all manner of evil. Rather, he should take care to be generous to the deserving poor, clothing and feeding them from the best, as it is written (Leviticus 3:16), "all the fat is the Lord's." And his reward will be the good hidden away for him, of which it is said, "no eye has seen it, O God, besides You; He works for him who waits for Him" (Isaiah 64:3).
Orchot Tzadikim 18:2: Stinginess. This trait is disgraceful in most of its effects. And of the stingy man Solomon, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 23:6), "do not eat the bread of him who has an evil eye."
Orchot Tzadikim 18:3: And these are the traits of the narrow-eyed man: he does not give charity, and does not show mercy to the poor. And when he has business dealings with his fellow, he is overly exacting with him, and yields nothing at all to him. He feeds no one and clothes no one, and no person benefits from him. He has no trust in the One who gives him his money, and he is hated by his fellow creatures. He does not go to any trouble for the commandments, and does not acquire for himself a teacher or a companion, and through this he is left empty of Torah and commandments.
Orchot Tzadikim 18:4: And if he is stingy with his own body, this too is bad and bitter, in that he does no kindness for people. And worst of all evils is when he is stingy with his wisdom or his books, since he loses nothing at all by sharing it — for wisdom is like fire, which loses nothing if lamps or other fires are kindled from it. And of him it is said (Proverbs 11:26), "he who withholds grain, the people shall curse him." But of the generous man it is said (ibid.), "but a blessing shall be on the head of him who sells [supplies] it." The plain meaning of the verse speaks of charity, and the parable applies to his wisdom.
Orchot Tzadikim 18:5: And the good side of this trait is that he does not squander his money on vanities, and sometimes refrains from great transgressions. And because he denies himself good things, he does not have the haughtiness that the generous man has, since from an abundance of good and pleasure a person may kick against his Maker. Therefore let a person be exacting with himself, and be generous where it is fitting to be generous, and where it is not fitting to be generous let him be stingy and tight-fisted. And let him weigh all this on the scales of the Torah.
Orchot Tzadikim 18:6: And let him learn from Jacob our father, who was stingy beyond compare, as it is said (Genesis 32:25), "and Jacob was left alone" — and our Sages of blessed memory said that he had forgotten some small jars and went back for them. This teaches that the righteous hold their money dearer than their own bodies, because they do not stretch out their hand in robbery (Chullin 91a). See what great stinginess this was, that a rich man like Jacob, peace upon him, had to go back for small jars! And we find elsewhere that he was forbearing beyond compare, as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Shemot Rabbah 31:17) on "in my grave which I have dug for myself" (Genesis 50:5) — this teaches that Jacob took all the silver and gold he had brought from Laban's house and made it into a heap, and said to Esau: take it for your share in the [Cave of Machpelah]. Is there such forbearance as this?!
Orchot Tzadikim 18:7: Therefore let a person learn from this not to squander in vain and without need. But in a place of a commandment, such as charity and other commandments that depend on money, such as acquiring a teacher and a companion and books, let him be very forbearing, in order to attain the supernal virtues, to return the soul to a place of purity, that it be bound in the bond of life, as it is written (1 Samuel 25:29), "and the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bond of life."
Orchot Tzadikim 19:2: Remembrance is a trait without which the world could not endure. For all the dealings of this world depend entirely on remembrance, for a person would not trust his fellow or lend to him if he did not remember. And all matters in the world, such as buying and selling, if people forgot their words, they could not conduct business, or make agreements between themselves without remembrance. There is no need to elaborate on this, for it is known to all. Therefore let a person take up this trait to make use of it in all matters. For remembrance is a fence for truth: how else would he remember the vows he made to fulfill? And if there is some matter between him and his fellow, he should remember the matter and not change his words. If he was told a secret and instructed not to reveal it, he should remember his instruction and not reveal it.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:3: If he borrowed money from his fellow or borrowed the vessels of his house, let him remember how much money he borrowed, and be exacting in his accounting, and repay everything. And whoever has many affairs and is preoccupied should be very careful not to borrow money, or borrow items from people, for since he is preoccupied, he will forget everything and not remember. If his fellow did him a kindness, let him remember it so that he may repay him. And regarding charity: he must remember the poor and bring their distress to mind, and through this help them. And if he comes to testify in court about what he saw and knew, a person must be very careful to remember, and not diminish or add to what he saw and knew. See how the Holy One, blessed be He, warned about remembrance, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:11), "take heed lest you forget the Lord your God, in not keeping His commandments, His judgments, and His statutes." And this is a great thing: to remember the Blessed Lord in all one's deeds. And so David said (Psalms 16:8), "I have set the Lord always before me."
Orchot Tzadikim 19:4: Remembrance is a supreme virtue, and it is a vessel that upholds all the commandments and the entire Torah. Of tzitzit it is said (Numbers 15:39-40), "and you shall remember all the commandments of the Lord, and do them... that you may remember and do all My commandments." Of tefillin it is said (Exodus 13:9), "and it shall be to you a sign upon your hand, and a memorial between your eyes, that the law of the Lord may be in your mouth"; and it is written (Deuteronomy 16:12), "and you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt, and you shall observe and do these statutes."
Orchot Tzadikim 19:5: And since everything depends on remembrance, I must write thirty things that you should remember twice each day, and bring them into the depths of your heart and your thoughts. Do not merely recite them with your mouth, but write them upon the tablet of your heart; then your service will be accepted before the Blessed Omnipresent, and you will find favor and kindness before Him.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:6: The first remembrance: that you remember how the Blessed Creator brought you forth from nothing into being. And remember the good He has done for you from your beginning until this day, and how He raised you up and exalted you above all creatures. And all this He did for you though He was not obligated to do it for you, but did it for you gratis, and out of the abundance of His kindness He bestowed all this upon you, and for this you are obligated to thank the Blessed Creator.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:7: The second: that he remember the kindnesses of the Blessed Lord, in that he is whole in his limbs. And let him think: if one limb had been ill, and a physician came and healed it, how submissive he would be and how grateful to that physician! How much more so should he do this before the Blessed Lord, who made him whole.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:8: The third: that he remember the kindnesses of the Blessed Lord, who gave him wisdom and knowledge. And let him think: if he were a fool, tearing his garments, how ruined his affairs would be, and he would be worth nothing at all. And if a physician were to heal his foolishness, how fitting it would be to praise him! How much more so [should he praise] the Blessed Creator, whose Name be blessed.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:9: The fourth: that he remember the good the exalted God has given him, that He gave him His holy Torah to teach him His straight ways, so that he attain the service of the exalted God; and let him be favorably disposed to thank the exalted Lord God for it, through which he will attain to be illuminated by the light of life, to enjoy the splendor of the Divine Presence.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:10: The fifth: that he remember the mercy of the exalted God, who had mercy upon him to place His pure Torah in his hand. And if a king of flesh and blood sent him a letter, and he read the whole letter, and there was something in it he did not understand, how distressed he would be over this, that he did not know what the king had commanded him. And there is no doubt that if even the smallest of the small were in his place and could explain to him what he did not understand, he would hasten to go to him, and would not be ashamed. How much more so should he do this regarding the Torah of our God.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:11: The sixth: that he remember if there is anything in which he transgresses what his Maker commanded him. And let him think about this: that all the things the Blessed Creator created perform His commandment — the donkey bears its burden, the horse and the ox plow, and there is not a single day that they rebel against their master. The sun does, every day, what the exalted God commanded it, and if there were a single day it did not shine and there was darkness, how great a wonder it would be in the eyes of the world! Or if the waters of the sea were to cross the boundary the Holy One, blessed be He, gave them, they would destroy the world. Or if the earth did not give its produce and its fruits, the whole world would die. Now see that all things perform their mission — how is a person not ashamed to accustom his limbs, which were created to keep the Torah, to change their purpose and accustom his limbs instead to transgress the Torah?
Orchot Tzadikim 19:12: The seventh: that he remember, in worldly matters, a servant who saw that his master does good to him and supplies his needs — how much that servant must accept upon himself the awe and love of his master, and submit before him, and strive with all his strength to find favor in his master's eyes. How much more so should a person accept upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, and regard himself as a servant submissive before his master, and show no domineering or haughtiness in himself.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:13: The eighth: that he remember how diligent and exerting all the king's servants are in his service. And if the king's servants perform an act for the king, something requiring wisdom and counsel, behold, they clear their minds of everything else, and set all their thoughts and their wisdom to perform the king's matter with understanding and wisdom, and with all the intent and all the heart they are capable of. And if it comes to praising the king and crediting him with the good he has done for him, whether writing him a letter or standing before him orally, he will search his heart for eloquent and fitting language to praise the king with. How much more so should one do this before the King of kings, that he set all his intent on the service of the Blessed Lord, to perform it according to its law and to beautify it. And behold, we may divide every deed of the service of the Blessed Lord into three parts: the first, the duty of the heart alone — if he occupies his thought with the unity of the Blessed Lord, let him clear his heart of all his other thoughts, and let his devotion be entirely to God alone. The second, the occupation of both heart and limbs, such as in prayer — let him clear his heart of all his affairs, and stand with great intent before the great exalted God. The third, such as making a lulav and tzitzit and the like, which are commandments of the limbs alone, where the essential intent is not as in prayer, for the essence of prayer is the intent, but the essence of these is in the limbs without the heart — even so, before performing the commandment, let him remember for whose sake he performs it, and perform it with a beautification of the commandment worth up to a third [more of his money] (Bava Kamma 9b), for the sake of the Master of the worlds.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:14: The ninth: that a person remember that he has a wife whom he loves as his own soul, or a son whom he loves with all his heart, and he constantly labors to obtain all their needs and do all their wishes; and he does not do this because he fears them, or because they will do good to him for doing their will, but does it out of the abundance of the love he feels for them. How much more so should he do this before the exalted God, directing all his deeds toward His great Name alone, and not perform the commandments out of love of people or fear of them, or hoping to receive some benefit. Rather, he should devote all his deeds to His great Name alone, and not associate anything else with it.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:15: The tenth: that he remember what all his deeds have been until this day — whether he occupied himself with the service of his Maker or with following his own inclination. And he must remember every day how much he has done in the service of the Blessed Lord and how much he has rebelled against Him. And let him always set his heart to occupy himself more with the service of the Blessed Lord than with his own needs. And if he has not occupied himself all his days with the service of the Blessed Creator, let him at least occupy himself with the service of the Blessed Lord from now on.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:16: The eleventh: that he remember how diligent and swift he is in his affairs to gather wealth, thinking of it day and night, and cares to love only whoever will help him accumulate silver and gold. And it is possible that his labor will be in vain, that he will lose everything, or that his wealth will be to his own harm, or that he may die soon; nonetheless he toils so much. If so, what shall he do for his soul, which endures forever and ever? And further: how much more are you obligated to set your affairs in order, and be diligent to always remember to purify them and polish them with the merit that endures forever and ever, for all eternity. And now see what a difference there is between the two worlds, and the superiority of the one over the other, "as the advantage of light over darkness" (Ecclesiastes 2:13).
